Azure Policy Linter

Make linter results useful.

This skill reads a policy and its linter results, removes warnings that do not matter, combines repeated warnings, and suggests what to do next.

Understands the policy Easy-to-read results Ready for PR comments

Why this is needed

Not every warning needs a policy change.

The linter lacks context

It sees the policy text, but it does not know why the policy was written or how it is assigned.

Warnings can repeat

Several warnings may describe the same problem and should become one clear comment.

Some fixes are choices

A change may alter what the policy does. The skill should ask for a decision instead of pretending there is one safe fix.

What the skill does

It turns a long warning list into a short action list.

1. Read

Read one policy and the matching linter results.

->

2. Understand

Check the policy's purpose, effect, conditions, and existing safeguards.

->

3. Simplify

Remove noise, combine related warnings, and give the safest next step.

Possible answers

Every result gets one clear next step.

Make this edit

There is a clear change that keeps the policy's behavior the same.

Choose an option

The author must decide how the policy should behave.

Check first

More information is needed before changing the policy.

No change

The warning does not apply or the policy already handles it correctly.

Exact duplicate findings

I ran the linter on all 2,252 policies to learn the common patterns. I did not run the skill on all 2,252 policies. The skill tests used focused examples and one real policy with 39 findings.

The test examples

I tested nine different situations.

Simple fixes

Repeated warnings and two warnings solved by the same small edit.

Policy intent

Warnings that may be correct because the policy deliberately covers several resource types or deploys by default.

Alias warnings

Fields that may be missing or unavailable in older API versions.

Broken or incomplete input

A critical linter failure, old results that no longer match the policy, and console output missing details.

Finding the right result

A policy with results for several files, where guessing would be unsafe.

Lots of warnings

A real policy with 39 findings to check whether the skill combines them sensibly.

How the testing worked

Each situation was run several times.

5x

Each test was repeated because an AI can give a different answer to the same request.

Full instructions

The AI received the skill and the required output format.

Comparison runs

The AI received only the output format, or no special help at all.

There were 135 first-round runs. After improving the instructions, I ran 40 more tests on the situations that had problems.

What the scores mean

Three simple questions were checked.

Can software read it?

Did the answer use the exact JSON format needed by a future PR-comment tool?

Did it pass every check?

Did it account for every warning, combine only related warnings, use the right policy locations, and handle errors safely?

Was the advice good?

Did it correctly decide between an edit, a choice, more research, or no change?

Good final advice
39/40

Combining related warnings is expected and does not lower this score. A run fails when it loses a warning or combines warnings that need different decisions. The 39/40 score uses corrected grading rules because two original expected answers were wrong.

What I fixed

The first test round found clear instruction gaps.

  • Stop when the linter itself failed.
  • Do not guess when results may be for another file.
  • Say when old results no longer match the policy.
  • Do not call behavior-changing edits automatic fixes.
  • Handle policies supplied without their outer Azure resource wrapper.
  • Point to the exact policy sections that support the answer.

What still needs work

The AI can organize the same warnings differently.

39/40

Runs gave good advice after the grading corrections.

1 miss

One run combined two different identity warnings that should have stayed separate.

The answer remains readable by software, but repeated runs may group warnings or explain the evidence differently. A future pipeline should not expect identical wording every time.
